sections.title: 4. Understand executable net risk
sections.body: The theoretical size must be rounded to the minimum and step and is constrained by maximum size, margin, and costs. The displayed net risk may therefore be slightly below the target.

callout.title: Risk-based sizing needs a valid stop
callout.body: Cash and percentage risk depend on stop distance. Define where the trade is invalid first, then size the position to fit the risk.

success: You can explain the difference between fixed size and risk-based sizing.
Calculated size changes when the stop distance changes.
Executable risk does not exceed the preset limit.

faq.q: Why is displayed risk below 1% after I enter 1%?
faq.a: Size must follow the minimum and step. TradeReplay normally adjusts toward an executable size that does not exceed the limit.

faq.q: Why is the calculated size zero?
faq.a: The target risk may be smaller than the risk of the minimum size, or margin may be insufficient. Check account parameters, stop distance, and instrument specifications.

faq.q: Are fees included in risk?
faq.a: Executable risk accounts for configured trading costs where possible. More accurate costs produce a result closer to the real rules.

articles.title: Set and modify stop loss and take profit
articles.summary: Enter protection by points or price and modify it after the position opens.
articles.outcome: You will set and modify stops and targets before or after entry and identify invalid protection prices.
before: Open a replay chart.
Know the instrument’s quote precision and minimum price increment.

sections.title: 1. Enter points or a price
sections.body: Enter a distance in points or an exact target price. With points, TradeReplay converts the distance according to direction. With price, make sure it is on the correct side of entry.

sections.title: 2. Check the directional relationship
sections.body: A long stop is normally below entry and its target above; a short position is the reverse. TradeReplay blocks submission or asks for correction if the direction is invalid, the level is too close, or precision is wrong.

sections.title: 3. Modify an open position
sections.body: Choose Modify from the position panel or a protection line, enter the new value, and confirm. Verify the new stop or target in both the position panel and on the chart.

sections.title: 4. Understand triggering
sections.body: During replay, protection triggers according to the replay mode, Bid/Ask, spread, and instrument rules. Real ticks and synthesized control points can produce a different intrabar order.

callout.title: A stop defines invalidation; it is not an arbitrary cash button
callout.body: Choose the stop from market structure first, then control the amount at risk with position sizing.

success: Chart protection lines match the entered values.
Protection prices are on the correct side for the position.
The position panel shows the new stop or target after modification.

faq.q: Why can’t I save the stop price?
faq.a: Check its direction, minimum distance, quote precision, and the current price. A stop cannot be placed on an invalid side.

faq.q: What if the same bar touches both stop and target?
faq.a: The result depends on the intrabar order provided by the replay mode. Use finer data when the order matters, and keep the mode consistent in comparisons.

faq.q: Why did percentage risk change after moving the stop?
faq.a: The position size is already fixed, so changing stop distance changes the remaining risk directly.

articles.title: Use order-discipline rules to block impulsive trades
articles.summary: Require a stop, trading system, and entry reason before an order can be placed.
articles.outcome: You will configure order gates that block submission when a required stop, system, or entry reason is missing.
before: Create or select a trading system.
Decide which information is mandatory for every trade.

sections.title: 1. Open order-discipline settings
sections.body: Open the trading or discipline area in Settings and find the pre-order checks. A normal checklist is a reminder; only items enabled as discipline gates block submission.

sections.title: 2. Choose mandatory items
sections.body: Require a stop, trading system, entry reason, or other information that your process needs. Start with a few critical items instead of turning every optional field into paperwork.

steps.title: Leave one item blank on purpose
steps.body: Try to place an order in a replay session and confirm that the missing requirement is shown.

steps.title: Complete it and retry
steps.body: Fill the missing item, then submit again.

steps.title: Check History
steps.body: Confirm that the system and reason were saved with the trade for later statistics and review.

sections.title: 4. Turn the gate into a stable process
sections.body: Every discipline rule should map to an action you can execute. Review common block reasons. If an item is repeatedly filled with meaningless text, improve the rule definition instead of bypassing it.

callout.title: A checklist is not automatically an order gate
callout.body: Trading-system checks can be used only for review. Enable the matching condition in order discipline if it must block an order.

success: An order is blocked when a mandatory item is missing.
The message identifies what is missing.
After completion, the order submits normally and saves its context.

faq.q: Why can I still trade when a checklist exists?
faq.a: The checklist may be for recording only. Enable the mandatory gate in order-discipline settings.

faq.q: Do discipline rules change historical trades?
faq.a: No. They affect future order entry only.

faq.q: What if too many gates interrupt practice?
faq.a: Keep only a few critical conditions and rewrite vague rules as actions that can be judged clearly.

articles.title: Understand futures open, close-yesterday, and close-today fees
articles.summary: Configure the three commission rates and understand complete round-trip cost.
articles.outcome: You will configure open, close-yesterday, and close-today fees separately and understand the cost of a futures round trip.
before: Obtain the current fee rules from the exchange or futures broker.
Confirm whether fees are charged per contract, by notional percentage, or another method.
Understand how the instrument defines a trading day.

sections.title: 1. Why there are three fees
sections.body: Open is charged when a position is established. Close yesterday closes a position opened on an earlier trading day. Close today closes a position opened during the current trading day. The three rates may differ.

sections.title: 2. Determine today and yesterday by trading day
sections.body: A night session and a calendar day are not always the same. Determine whether a position is “today” from the market’s trading-day rules, not simply the computer date.

sections.title: 3. Enter the fees in account parameters
sections.body: Enter open, close-yesterday, and close-today costs for the instrument, then verify the contract multiplier and fee method. Some metals may have a lower close-today rate, while some equity-index futures may have a much higher one. Always use current rules.

sections.title: 4. Verify with a small sample
sections.body: Simulate a same-day open and close and a later-day close. Check the opening fee, closing fee, and net P&L in History. Complete round-trip cost is the opening fee plus the applicable closing fee.

callout.title: Do not keep using outdated rates
callout.body: Exchanges and brokers can change their standards. Recheck them before a cost-sensitive backtest or practice session.

success: All three fee types are configured separately.
Same-day and later-day closes use the appropriate rules.
History net P&L includes the corresponding fees.

faq.q: Is close-today always more expensive than close-yesterday?
faq.a: No. Rules vary by instrument and period. Use the current exchange and broker standards.

faq.q: Why can a position opened at night still count as today the next morning?
faq.a: A futures trading day may begin on the previous calendar evening. Use the trading-day boundary rather than midnight.

faq.q: What does an incorrect fee affect?
faq.a: It affects net P&L, the equity curve, Profit Factor, expectancy, and backtest conclusions.

articles.title: Understand margin, available funds, and maximum size
articles.summary: Understand equity, used margin, margin usage, and the maximum executable position size.
articles.outcome: You will understand the relationship between equity, used margin, available funds, margin usage, and maximum order size.
before: Confirm the contract multiplier and margin rate.
Set the account balance and currency.
Understand that unrealized P&L changes equity.

sections.title: 1. Four core values
sections.body: Equity is balance plus unrealized P&L. Used margin is occupied by current positions. Available funds are the remaining capacity for risk or new positions. Margin usage shows occupied margin relative to equity.

sections.title: 2. Margin per contract
sections.body: For futures with a fixed margin rate, margin per contract is normally estimated from price, contract multiplier, and margin rate. Price changes, contract rules, and account parameters affect the result.

sections.title: 3. Maximum order size
sections.body: TradeReplay estimates the maximum new size from current equity, margin per contract, occupied size, and instrument limits, then applies the size step. As unrealized losses grow, the maximum declines.

sections.title: 4. Margin is not a stop loss
sections.body: Margin determines whether a position can be held, not whether its risk is reasonable. Even if the system permits a large size, use stop distance and per-trade risk to limit the position first.

callout.title: Simulated values depend on your configured rules
callout.body: TradeReplay calculations support practice and backtesting; they do not replace a broker’s real-time risk controls. Use the live account for current margin rates, price limits, and temporary adjustments.

success: You can explain the difference between balance and equity.
You can see how positions consume margin.
You do not treat maximum order size as a recommended position.

faq.q: Why can’t I place an order even though the account has a balance?
faq.a: Available funds may be insufficient, or the order may exceed the allowed margin usage. Check unrealized loss, margin rate, and size.

faq.q: Why does price change margin?
faq.a: When margin is based on contract value, price changes margin per contract; unrealized P&L also changes equity.

faq.q: Why isn’t maximum size a whole number?
faq.a: Markets use different minimum sizes and steps. The final value is converted to a quantity the instrument can submit.

articles.title: How TradeReplay handles liquidation
articles.summary: Understand the liquidation threshold, the no-liquidation option, and the resulting trade record.
articles.outcome: You will understand when simulated liquidation triggers, what it does, and the risk of disabling liquidation simulation.
before: Configure margin or leverage parameters for the account.
The session has a position that consumes margin.

sections.title: 1. When liquidation triggers
sections.body: TradeReplay triggers liquidation when unrealized loss reduces equity to the simulated risk threshold. Fixed-margin futures usually compare equity with used margin; other account types use their configured stop-out parameters.

sections.title: 2. What happens after the trigger
sections.body: The simulator closes the affected positions at available prices, records the liquidation reason, fills, and costs, and updates the balance. The exit reason is available in History.

sections.title: 3. The no-liquidation option
sections.body: With liquidation simulation disabled, market replay and unrealized results continue, but TradeReplay does not close the position at the margin threshold. This can be used to study an extreme path; it does not mean a live account can absorb unlimited loss.

sections.title: 4. Control risk before liquidation
sections.body: Use stops, risk-based sizing, and lower margin usage. Liquidation is a final safety mechanism, not a normal exit method.

callout.title: Live broker rules can be more complex
callout.body: A live account may also be affected by margin calls, intraday changes, price limits, and liquidity. The simulation reflects only the current session parameters.

success: You can find the liquidation threshold or no-liquidation setting.
A liquidated trade has a clear exit reason in History.
You understand that the simulation is not a promise of live-broker behavior.

faq.q: Why did liquidation happen before the balance reached zero?
faq.a: Margin risk controls trigger when equity approaches used margin or another configured threshold; they do not wait for a zero balance.

faq.q: What happens to the balance when liquidation is disabled?
faq.a: The position continues to produce unrealized results as the market moves. This mode is for research, not a representation of tradable live conditions.

faq.q: Why is the liquidation fill different from the threshold?
faq.a: After triggering, the simulator uses the next available quote together with spread and replay granularity, so the fill may differ.

articles.title: Find a trade in History
articles.summary: Filter trades by source, date, instrument, direction, result, and tag.
articles.outcome: You will combine History filters to locate a trade quickly and restore the complete list afterward.
before: At least one replay session, backtest, or live account contains trades.
Know the approximate date, instrument, or account source of the target trade.

sections.title: 1. Narrow the account source first
sections.body: Open Review → History and first select the account, replay session, or source type. A precise source makes later date and instrument filters clearer.

sections.title: 2. Combine filters
sections.body: Narrow the list by date, instrument, direction, P&L result, and tag. Multiple filters usually apply together, so check for excessive restrictions when no results appear.

sections.title: 3. Open the trade details
sections.body: Select the target row to inspect open and close times, prices, size, fees, net P&L, system, reason, tags, and notes. Open the chart preview when you need market context.

sections.title: 4. Clear the filters
sections.body: After finding the trade, clear or reset the filters and confirm that the complete list returns. Otherwise, a filtered view can look like missing data on your next visit.

callout.title: Stable tags make filtering useful
callout.body: Use one tag for the same behavior. For example, do not split one idea across “chasing,” “late entry,” and “FOMO” unless they have distinct definitions.

success: You can find the target range by account and date.
You can add instrument, direction, result, or tag filters.
The complete trade list returns after filters are cleared.

faq.q: Why is History empty?
faq.a: Clear all filters, then check the account scope and date. If it is still empty, confirm that the trade was closed or the import completed.

faq.q: Does an open position appear among completed trades?
faq.a: Open positions and complete closed trades use different views and statistics. Check the corresponding account or position area.

faq.q: Do filters modify data?
faq.a: No. Filters change only the current display; they do not delete or edit trades.

articles.title: Open the chart preview for a trade
articles.summary: View statement or system market data, move between trades, and continue into a fuller review.
articles.outcome: You will open a chart preview from History, move between trades, and know when market data needs to be added or matched.
before: The target trade exists in History.
Local bar data should cover the instrument and trade dates.

sections.title: 1. Open the preview from a trade
sections.body: Select a trade in Review → History and open Chart preview. The chart loads around the entry and exit and marks direction and position.

sections.title: 2. Understand the market-data source
sections.body: Use statement-provided market data when it exists. Otherwise, use matched system or custom data. Reference data provides review context and does not rewrite original fill prices.

sections.title: 3. Move between trades
sections.body: Use Previous and Next to browse trades in the current filtered result. Keeping the same zoom and timeframe helps compare the same system or behavior.

sections.title: 4. Continue to a fuller review
sections.body: Open the review map when you need a wider range, trade lines, or the complete account process. Create a separate replay session if you want to simulate the decisions again.

callout.title: Reference bars are not the broker’s tick-by-tick quotes
callout.body: Data sources can differ in time zone, spread, or small price details. The original statement remains the source of truth for fills.

success: Entry and exit markers appear in the preview.
You can move to the previous or next trade.
You know to match market data rather than edit a fill when chart data is missing.

faq.q: Why does the preview report missing bar data?
faq.a: The instrument may not be matched, or local data may not cover the trade date. Complete instrument matching and prepare the required range.

faq.q: Is it normal for the chart price to differ slightly from the fill?
faq.a: It can be. Reference data and broker fills may differ because of source, Bid/Ask, spread, and time zone.

faq.q: Can the preview modify a trade?
faq.a: No. It shows context. Trade facts come from replay matching or the original statement and should not be rewritten on the chart.

articles.title: Create and manage a live account
articles.summary: Set the account name, broker, currency, and custom identifier.
articles.outcome: You will create a live account for statement imports and safely update its name, broker, and custom identifier.
before: Have the account currency, platform, and broker name ready.
If you plan to import a statement, confirm the account number and currency in the report first.

sections.title: 1. Create a live account
sections.body: Go to Review → Accounts and choose New live account. Enter a clear account name, platform or broker, currency, and custom identifier.

sections.title: 2. Add details you can recognize
sections.body: The account name helps with everyday identification. The broker and identifier distinguish similar accounts. The currency determines how balances and statistics are displayed. Do not rely on the same nickname for several accounts.

sections.title: 3. Manage the account
sections.body: Use the account menu to edit display details and review history, cash flows, and imports. Renaming an account does not change existing trades.

sections.title: 4. Select the correct account during import
sections.body: The import preview shows the detected account number and currency. Append data only when both belong to the same live account. Otherwise, create a new account.

callout.title: Do not merge different account numbers or currencies
callout.body: An incorrect merge distorts balances, cash flows, and statistics. Check the original report before importing.

success: The new live account appears on the Accounts page.
Its currency, broker, and identifier match the original account.
Future imports clearly offer the correct choice between creating and appending.

faq.q: Does the account name have to match the broker?
faq.a: No. It is your own display name, but including the broker and purpose makes the account easier to identify.

faq.q: Can I freely change the currency after choosing the wrong one?
faq.a: Currency affects balances and statistics. Once trades exist, do not change it merely for display convenience. Verify the original account and, when necessary, import again into the correct account.

faq.q: Is the custom identifier uploaded?
faq.a: Account details stay in your local library. Whether they are included in a backup depends on the backup settings you configure.

articles.title: Export and import MT4 or MT5 trade history
articles.summary: Select a platform history report, review the preview, account, and instruments, then complete the import.
articles.outcome: Your MT4 or MT5 trade history will be stored in a live account and available in History, Statistics, and chart review.
before: Export a report containing the complete trade history from MT4 or MT5.
Select one report at a time. Import a newer report later when you need to append updates.
Importing does not modify the source report. Keep an untouched copy before you begin.

sections.title: 1. Export a history report from the platform
sections.body:
In MT4 or MT5 Account History, select the required date range and export the history report offered by the platform. Include the complete history where possible so that statistics do not cover only part of the account period.

Do not use a screenshot or a manually prepared spreadsheet as the report. TradeReplay reads the platform, account, currency, fills, and cash flows from the exported report.

steps.title: Open Import
steps.body: Go to Review → Accounts, select Import, then choose MT4/MT5.

steps.title: Choose the file
steps.body: Select the history report you just exported and wait for parsing to finish.

steps.title: Do not click repeatedly
steps.body: A large report can take a moment. Keep the window open while parsing progress is visible.

sections.title: 3. Review the import preview
sections.body:
Confirm the platform, broker, account, currency, date range, trade count, and cash flows.

If TradeReplay recognizes an existing account, you can append to it. Otherwise, create a new account. Do not decide by display name alone; verify both the account number and currency.

sections.title: 4. Check instrument and chart-data matching
sections.body:
TradeReplay tries to match broker instrument names to available market data. Broker prefixes, suffixes, and custom symbols may require manual selection.

Unmatched means the instrument is not yet identified. Missing bars means it is identified but local data does not cover the review period. Source unavailable means no reference source is currently available for automatic download.

callout.title: Do not match instruments merely because their codes look similar
callout.body: Different indices, micro contracts, and standard contracts can have different contract sizes. Verify the instrument specification before saving a mapping.

sections.title: 5. Complete the import and check the result
sections.body:
Start the import after approving the preview. Duplicate fills are removed when appending.

When it finishes, open the account and check the trading calendar, equity curve, instruments, cash flows, and account details. Open one trade and confirm its time, direction, price, and fees.

success: The platform, currency, and trade count are correct in the account details.
The imported live trades can be filtered in History.
Trades for matched instruments can open a chart preview.

faq.q: Will importing the same report twice create duplicate trades?
faq.a: Append imports are deduplicated by trade identifiers. Still check the new-item count in the preview so that two different accounts are not merged by mistake.

faq.q: Why is a positive entry in the report classified as a deposit?
faq.a: Rebates or promotions may need a matching keyword under Settings → Data. Add the keyword, then import the relevant batch again.

faq.q: Why are trade times several hours apart?
faq.a: Broker report time, chart display time zone, and underlying UTC data are separate concepts. See “Chart time differs from statement time by several hours” first.

articles.title: Import CFMMC futures daily or monthly statements
articles.summary: Import several CFMMC files together and restore fills, cash flows, and positions carried between months.
articles.outcome: You will review futures fills, fees, cash flows, and positions by trading day, and open chart review for matched contracts.
before: Have the daily or monthly statement files obtained from China Futures Market Monitoring Center.
You can select several files at once. Keep their dates continuous where possible.
Reports can contain sensitive account information. Process them only on your own computer.

sections.title: 1. Prepare the CFMMC files
sections.body:
If the files are already on your computer, collect the daily or monthly reports you need. Do not manually change their worksheet structure.

You can also open the CFMMC download page from the online window in TradeReplay. Enter usernames, passwords, verification codes, and two-factor authentication yourself. The tutorial and the app do not record them.

callout.title: Complete sensitive steps yourself
callout.body: Never include passwords, verification codes, or identity details in tutorial screenshots or support requests.

steps.title: Open account import
steps.body: Go to Review → Accounts → Import and choose CFMMC.

steps.title: Select the files
steps.body: You can select several daily or monthly reports. TradeReplay parses and groups them by trading day.

steps.title: Wait for every file
steps.body: Do not close the window while a larger batch is being processed. Wait until the file and trading-day counts in the preview stop changing.

sections.title: 3. Check the preview
sections.body:
Review the file count, trading days, fill count, realized profit and loss, fees, open positions, deposits, withdrawals, and credit entries.

When a monthly statement includes a position carried from the previous month, TradeReplay estimates its opening price from the available settlement and profit data. Gaps in dates or fields may require manual verification.

sections.title: 4. Match futures-contract market data
sections.body:
TradeReplay prioritizes the specific delivery contract instead of substituting only a continuous contract. If local data is missing, follow the prompt to download the relevant contract.

A 9999 continuous contract is useful for continuous observation. For fill-by-fill statement review, use the specific contract that was actually traded whenever possible.

callout.title: Do not identify a contract by its product name alone
callout.body: Delivery months for the same product have different prices and liquidity. Positions carried across months require particular care.

sections.title: 5. Import and check the account
sections.body:
Start the import after confirming the preview. Then use the account details to inspect its calendar, equity curve, instruments, cash flows, and archived statements.

Spot-check one close-today fill, one close-previous-day fill, and one carried position. Confirm direction, price, fee, and opening date.

success: The file, trading-day, and fill counts agree with the statements.
Cash flows distinguish deposits, withdrawals, and credit entries.
Matched contracts open a trade chart and carried positions have verifiable opening details.

faq.q: Can daily and monthly reports be imported together?
faq.a: Yes. Check overlapping dates and duplicate ranges in the preview first. Appending removes duplicates, but you should still confirm the final new-item count.

faq.q: Why is the close-today fee much higher than the close-previous-day fee?
faq.a: Some exchanges and products apply a separate close-today rate. TradeReplay records open, close-previous-day, and close-today fees separately, so one uniform rate cannot explain every fill.

faq.q: Why is the opening price of a carried position different from what I remember?
faq.a: The app estimates it from available settlement and profit data. If an intermediate report is missing or the broker uses a special convention, verify it against the original statement.

articles.title: Check an import preview before continuing
articles.summary: Verify the account, currency, trades, cash flows, dates, and instruments before writing data to the wrong account.
articles.outcome: You will verify the account, currency, dates, trades, cash flows, and instruments before anything is written to the library.
before: Select an original MT4/MT5, CFMMC, or other supported report.
Keep the original report available for comparison.

sections.title: 1. Verify the account identity
sections.body: Start with the platform, broker, account number, and currency. When appending to an existing account, verify both the account number and currency rather than relying on a similar display name.

sections.title: 2. Verify counts and dates
sections.body: Check the number of files, date range, trades, cash flows, and open positions. For an append import, pay particular attention to whether the new count is reasonable.

sections.title: 3. Verify amounts
sections.body: Spot-check realized profit and loss, fees, deposits, withdrawals, credit entries, and rebates. A positive cash flow is not always a deposit. Add the required cash-flow keywords and parse again when necessary.

sections.title: 4. Verify instrument matching
sections.body: Review every unmatched instrument, missing-bar warning, and unavailable source. For futures, confirm the exact delivery month. For FX or CFDs, check broker prefixes and suffixes.

callout.title: Do not continue when the preview is wrong
callout.body: Return to the source file or account selection and resolve the cause. Cleaning up an incorrect account after import takes more work.

sections.title: 5. Spot-check after import
sections.body: After importing, use the account details and History to check at least one winning trade, one losing trade, and one trade with fees. Confirm that the total count matches the preview.

success: The account number, currency, and target account agree.
The trade and cash-flow counts agree with the original report.
Every unusual instrument is either resolved or intentionally left unmatched.

faq.q: Does the preview modify my library?
faq.a: No. Data is written only after you confirm the final import.

faq.q: Why is the new-item count lower than the report’s trade count?
faq.a: The report may include duplicates, non-trade cash flows, or fills that were already imported. Review the deduplication and classification results in the preview.

faq.q: Can I import with unmatched instruments?
faq.a: Yes. The trade facts can be retained and market data matched later, but those trades will not have a complete chart review until then.

articles.title: Match statement instruments to chart data
articles.summary: Distinguish unmatched instruments, missing bars, and unavailable sources, then use automatic or manual matching.
articles.outcome: You will understand the three matching states, connect statement instruments to the correct local chart data, and open a trade preview.
before: Trades have already been imported into a live account.
You know the real market or specific futures contract represented by the broker symbol.

sections.title: 1. Understand the statuses
sections.body: Unmatched: the instrument represented by the code is not yet known. Missing bars: the instrument is identified, but local data does not cover the trade dates. Source unavailable: the current catalog has no reference source that can be downloaded automatically.

sections.title: 2. Use automatic matching
sections.body: Automatic matching finds candidates from normalized codes, markets, and available data. Accept an unambiguous result directly. When several candidates appear, verify them manually.

sections.title: 3. Select the correct instrument manually
sections.body: Broker prefixes and suffixes, micro and standard contracts, and indices and CFDs cannot be identified from similar characters alone. Verify the contract specification, exchange, expiry month, and quote unit before saving the mapping.

sections.title: 4. Add chart data and verify the result
sections.body: If Missing bars remains after matching, download system data or import custom data that covers the trade dates. Return to History, open one trade, and check that its markers appear at reasonable times and prices.

callout.title: Prefer the specific contract over a continuous substitute
callout.body: For fill-by-fill futures review, match the contract actually traded whenever possible. Continuous contracts are useful for continuous observation, but their prices may differ.

success: The target no longer appears as unmatched.
Local chart data covers the trade dates.
The trade preview shows reasonable entry and exit positions.

faq.q: Why did automatic matching return no result?
faq.a: The broker code may contain a custom suffix, or the current data catalog may not cover that market. Search manually or import reference data.

faq.q: Can I map every delivery month to a continuous contract?
faq.a: That is not recommended for exact fill-by-fill review. Contracts differ in price and liquidity; use the traded delivery month first.

faq.q: What if I saved the wrong mapping?
faq.a: Open instrument mapping again, choose the correct data source, and check the trade preview. The original fill price is not rewritten by changing a mapping.

articles.title: Read the statistics overview and insights dashboard
articles.summary: Understand net profit and loss, win rate, payoff ratio, Profit Factor, expectancy, and maximum drawdown.
articles.outcome: You will interpret six core overview metrics correctly and avoid drawing strong conclusions from an inadequate sample.
before: Select an account or replay session containing closed trades.
Confirm that trades, fees, and the account currency are correct.
Use the same filters when comparing results.

sections.title: 1. Check the scope and insights first
sections.body: Go to Review → Statistics and confirm the account, dates, instruments, and systems in the filters. The insights dashboard summarizes strengths, risks, and behaviors in the current sample. Its conclusions apply only to the active filters.

sections.title: 2. Net P&L, win rate, and payoff ratio
sections.body:
Net P&L is the result after fees, swaps, and other costs. Win rate is the share of closed trades that made money. The payoff ratio compares the absolute average win with the absolute average loss.

A high win rate does not guarantee profit. A lower-win-rate approach can still produce a positive result when its average win is sufficiently large.

sections.title: 3. Profit Factor and expectancy
sections.body: Profit Factor = gross profit ÷ absolute gross loss. It shows how well profits cover losses. Expectancy is the average net result per trade. Always read both together with the trade count and time range.

sections.title: 4. Maximum drawdown
sections.body: Maximum drawdown is the largest decline in the equity curve from a previous peak to a later low. It represents the decline you might actually experience during a strategy, not the single largest losing trade.

sections.title: 5. Move from overview to diagnosis
sections.body: Start with the net result and drawdown. Then check whether win rate, payoff ratio, Profit Factor, and expectancy support the same conclusion. Finally, use behavior and distribution pages to locate the source, such as an instrument, session, direction, or tag.

callout.title: Do not rank very small samples
callout.body: One or two trades can make a ratio extreme. Collect a useful sample under the same rules before comparing versions or strategies.

success: You can explain the question answered by each of the six metrics.
The statistical scope matches the account and dates you intend to analyze.
You can continue from the overview to instrument, session, or behavior distributions to investigate a cause.

faq.q: Why is Profit Factor extremely large or unavailable?
faq.a: When gross loss is very small or zero, the denominator makes the ratio extreme or undefined. Read it together with the trade count and actual amounts.

faq.q: Why is expectancy low when net P&L is positive?
faq.a: A small number of large trades may account for the total profit. Averaged across every trade, the result can still be modest. Check the distribution and outliers.

faq.q: Why is maximum drawdown different from the largest losing trade?
faq.a: Drawdown measures the cumulative decline from an equity peak to a later low, which can be caused by several consecutive losses.

articles.title: Browse, search, and understand the indicator library
articles.summary: Find built-in and custom indicators and review their purpose, default parameters, formula syntax, and source.
articles.outcome: You will find a suitable built-in or custom indicator and understand its purpose, parameters, formula syntax, and source.
before: Know the problem you want to solve, such as trend, momentum, volatility, or volume.
Do not decide how to use an indicator from its name alone.

sections.title: 1. Browse the indicator library
sections.body: Go to Strategy → Indicators. Indicators are separated by built-in and custom sources. Browse categories or search by name, abbreviation, or purpose.

sections.title: 2. Read the indicator details
sections.body: Open an indicator and first review its purpose, outputs, default parameters, and suitable uses. Then read the source and implementation notes. A default parameter is a starting point, not the optimal answer for every market.

sections.title: 3. Use the formula syntax
sections.body: The formula example shows how to reference the indicator and its parameters in a strategy expression. After copying it, adapt the instrument, timeframe, and rules to your own use.

sections.title: 4. Manage custom indicators
sections.body: Create a custom indicator when you need to extend the library. After saving, check compatibility and error messages, then validate its output on a small data sample. Keep clear version names before making changes.

callout.title: Start with the question, not a pile of indicators
callout.body: Each indicator should answer one clear question. Several highly correlated indicators often repeat the same information.

success: You can search for and open the target indicator.
You can explain its main outputs and default parameters.
You can distinguish built-in and custom sources.

faq.q: Why can’t I find an indicator in search?
faq.a: Try its English abbreviation, full name, or purpose. You may also need to implement it as a custom indicator.

faq.q: Can I use the default parameters in a backtest?
faq.a: Use them as a baseline, then validate them over different periods so the result does not depend on one historical range.

faq.q: What should I do when an indicator looks wrong?
faq.a: Check data length, timeframe, parameter ranges, and any compatibility messages for the custom indicator.

articles.title: Create a trading system
articles.summary: Define its name, description, tags, entry checklist, risk rules, and exit rules.
articles.outcome: You will build a complete trading system with entry, risk, exit, and no-trade rules.
before: Write down the market, timeframe, and trade direction addressed by the system.
Prepare at least one entry condition that can be judged objectively.
Distinguish a discretionary trading system from an automated backtest strategy; they serve different purposes.

sections.title: 1. Add a name, description, and tags
sections.body: Go to Strategy → Systems and create a trading system. Use a name that distinguishes the market and version, describe when it applies, and add tags for filtering trades later.

sections.title: 2. Write the entry rules
sections.body: Break conditions into rule groups that can be judged, and mark them as automatic, semi-automatic, or manual. Avoid descriptions such as “feels good” or “nice pattern” that cannot be verified later.

sections.title: 3. Complete risk and exit rules
sections.body: The risk module should cover at least risk per trade, stop location, and scaling rules. The exit module should define profit-taking, trailing protection, time-based exits, or signal invalidation.

sections.title: 4. Add no-trade rules
sections.body: Record situations that require you to stand aside, such as before scheduled data, after consecutive losses, during abnormal spreads, or without a stop. No-trade rules often reduce impulsive decisions more effectively than adding more entry conditions.

sections.title: 5. Use the system in practice
sections.body: After saving, select the system and complete its checklist before placing an order. When the trade ends, record execution and deviations in History or the strategy journal.

callout.title: A system checklist records compliance by default
callout.body: To block orders when conditions are missing, enable an enforced gate in order discipline as well.

success: The system includes entry, risk, exit, and no-trade modules.
Every main rule can clearly pass or fail.
Practice trades can be linked to the system.

faq.q: What is the difference between a trading system and a backtest strategy?
faq.a: A trading system manages the complete discretionary decision and discipline process. A backtest strategy is an expression that historical data can execute. They can validate each other, but they are not the same object.

faq.q: Are more rules always better?
faq.a: No. Keep only conditions you can explain, execute, and review. Too many rules make hindsight selection easier.

faq.q: Will changing a system affect old trades?
faq.a: Old trades should retain the execution record from that time. Create a new version for major changes so that the results can be compared.

articles.title: Run your first strategy backtest
articles.summary: Select a strategy, market data, timeframe, dates, and capital, then run and review the result.
articles.outcome: You will choose a strategy, market data, timeframe, and cost assumptions, run a backtest, and open its read-only result for review.
before: Prepare market data that covers the backtest period.
Save an executable backtest strategy expression.
Prepare initial capital and cost assumptions that match the target market.

sections.title: 1. Select and save the strategy
sections.body: Go to Strategy → Backtest and select a saved strategy. Resolve expression and compatibility errors before running it. Unsaved temporary changes should not be used as a formal comparison baseline.

sections.title: 2. Set the data, timeframe, and dates
sections.body: Select the instrument data and strategy timeframe. Confirm that the start and end dates fall within the available range. The result archive locks the timeframe and parameters used for this run.

sections.title: 3. Set capital and costs
sections.body: Enter the initial capital, sizing method, spread, commission, slippage, or applicable futures costs. Ignoring costs can severely distort a high-frequency strategy.

sections.title: 4. Run the test and check the summary
sections.body: Submit the backtest and wait for it to finish. Review the trade count, net P&L, drawdown, and equity curve first, then check for no-trade results, insufficient data, or parameter errors.

sections.title: 5. Open the read-only review
sections.body: A backtest creates a read-only result archive. You can review it through Accounts, History, Statistics, and the review map, but you cannot place manual orders in that result.

callout.title: A backtest helps reject weak ideas; it does not guarantee future returns
callout.body: Validate the result on out-of-sample data and review trade count, cost sensitivity, and maximum drawdown.

success: The backtest completes over the selected dates and timeframe.
The result shows trades, an equity curve, and core statistics.
A read-only backtest archive appears on the Accounts page.

faq.q: Why did the backtest produce no trades?
faq.a: Check the strategy conditions, dates, timeframe, data completeness, and parameters. Use a deliberately looser test condition first to confirm the expression can trigger.

faq.q: Why can’t I place more orders in a backtest result?
faq.a: Backtest archives are for read-only review. Create a practice session with the same market data for manual training.

faq.q: Why does changing the timeframe change the result so much?
faq.a: The timeframe changes signals, intrabar paths, and sample size. Keep other parameters constant when comparing, and confirm that the strategy was designed for that timeframe.

articles.title: Configure DeepSeek or OpenAI
articles.summary: Save an API key, choose a model, and test the connection.
articles.outcome: You will configure Mentor with your own DeepSeek or OpenAI API key, select a model, and complete a connection test.
before: Create an API key with the chosen AI provider and confirm that the account is active.
API usage charges are billed directly by the provider.
Never expose a complete key in screenshots, chats, or support messages.

sections.title: 1. Open Mentor AI settings
sections.body: Go to Settings → Mentor AI and choose DeepSeek or OpenAI. Keys from different providers are not interchangeable.

sections.title: 2. Save the API key
sections.body: Paste the complete key without leading or trailing spaces. It is saved in the operating system’s secure credential storage, not in tutorial content or on TradeReplay servers.

sections.title: 3. Choose a model
sections.body: Select one of the currently available models. Speed, reasoning ability, context, and price are determined by the provider. For the first test, you can choose a lower-cost general model.

sections.title: 4. Test the connection
sections.body: Select Test connection. After it succeeds, save the settings and send a short question in Mentor. If it fails, check the key, provider balance, model access, network, and service status.

callout.title: Revoke an accidentally exposed key immediately
callout.body: If a complete key appears in a screenshot or public location, revoke it in the provider console and create a new one.

success: The connection test succeeds.
Mentor returns a short answer.
No complete API key appears in screenshots or notes.

faq.q: Does TradeReplay charge for API usage?
faq.a: When you bring your own key, the AI provider bills usage according to its own pricing and terms.

faq.q: Why does the test fail even though the key is correct?
faq.a: Check provider balance, model access, regional or network restrictions, and whether whitespace was pasted with the key.

faq.q: Why do I need to configure the key again on another computer?
faq.a: The key is stored in secure credentials on the current device. It is not copied to another computer with the ordinary library.

articles.title: Have an open conversation with Mentor
articles.summary: Ask Mentor questions and control the data sent to your AI provider.
articles.outcome: You will ask Mentor an actionable question, understand which TradeReplay data it can use, and control what is sent to the AI provider.
before: Configure and test DeepSeek or OpenAI.
Confirm that the selected account or practice records do not include private notes you do not want to send.
AI answers can be wrong. Verify important conclusions yourself.

sections.title: 1. Open Mentor
sections.body: Select the global Mentor entry. Its conversation panel appears beside the current workspace. Open conversation uses your own API key.

sections.title: 2. Ask a specific question
sections.body: State the goal, scope, and output format. For example: “Analyze only my latest 30 EURUSD practice trades, identify three repeated losing behaviors, and produce a checklist for my next session.” A specific question is easier to turn into action.

sections.title: 3. Understand the data scope
sections.body: Mentor can work with trades recorded in TradeReplay, including imported live trades and practice sessions. Check the selected account, filters, and context before sending. Do not add unrelated sensitive material to the prompt.

sections.title: 4. Verify the answer
sections.body: Ask Mentor which samples and evidence it used, then verify them in History and Statistics. Convert a suggestion into a measurable practice rule instead of copying it directly as a live-trading instruction.

callout.title: Mentor does not provide investment advice
callout.body: AI can misread data or generate inaccurate content. Use it to organize information, ask questions, and form hypotheses. You remain responsible for every decision.

success: The question states a clear account, scope, and goal.
You can identify the trades or statistics used as evidence.
At least one suggestion has been converted into a testable rule.

faq.q: Can Mentor see other files on my computer?
faq.a: It uses only the context the product supplies for the current request and does not browse unrelated computer files automatically. Do not paste unrelated sensitive information.

faq.q: Why does the answer disagree with the Statistics page?
faq.a: Check the account, dates, filters, and cost assumptions used by each. AI can also calculate or explain something incorrectly, so the original records and app statistics are the source of truth.

faq.q: Which Mentor features require Pro?
faq.a: Open conversation with your own API key is available directly. Productized analysis such as personalized review, patterns, trade insights, and strategy writing follows the current plan.

articles.title: Move the complete library to a new location
articles.summary: Safely migrate the database, market data, and local backups, then verify integrity.
articles.outcome: Your trade records, market data, review notes, and local backups will move together to another local drive or external drive.
before: Stop active downloads, CSV imports, backtests, and cloud backups.
Choose an empty destination folder with enough free space.
Do not use an iCloud, OneDrive, Dropbox, or other third-party sync folder as a live library.

sections.title: 1. Check the current library
sections.body:
Open Settings → Data. In Complete library, review the current path and the space used by the database, market data, and local backups.

The destination drive should have substantially more free space than the current total size.

sections.title: 2. Choose a new location
sections.body:
Select Change location and choose an empty folder. Migration copies the complete library, not only the database file.

If the destination already contains a TradeReplay library, use Open existing library instead of overwriting it with Change location.

callout.title: Do not move only tradereplay.db by hand
callout.body: Market data and local backups are part of the library too. Moving only the database can leave external references behind or make chart review lose its data.

sections.title: 3. Wait for copying and verification
sections.body:
Migration checks the library, copies the database, market data, and local backups, then verifies the new location. A large Tick dataset can take considerable time.

Do not quit TradeReplay, disconnect an external drive, or let the computer sleep before the app reports completion.

sections.title: 4. Verify the new library
bullets: Open Settings again and confirm that the current path is the new location.
Open a practice session and check its chart and trades.
Open a live account and check its trades, cash flows, and journal.
Handle any files left in the old location only after every check passes.

callout.title: For external-drive users
callout.body: Connect the drive before launching TradeReplay. Never disconnect the drive that contains the library while the app is running.

success: Settings shows the new library path.
Practice sessions, live accounts, journals, and market data all open normally.
TradeReplay still uses the new location after a restart.

faq.q: Why can’t I select a folder that already contains files?
faq.a: Migration requires an empty folder to avoid overwriting or mixing data. If that folder is an existing library, use Open existing library.

faq.q: Can I store the library on a NAS or synced drive?
faq.a: It is not recommended. A live database needs a stable local file system. You can use an external drive; for remote protection, use TradeReplay’s S3 cloud backup.

faq.q: What should I do if migration is interrupted?
faq.a: Do not combine the two locations manually. Reopen and verify the original library, then migrate again to a new empty folder.

articles.title: Restore a library from cloud backup
articles.summary: Restore user data from a snapshot in your own S3, COS, R2, or MinIO storage.
articles.outcome: Trades, accounts, strategies, settings, and journals from the selected snapshot will be restored to the local library. Official market data can be downloaded again when needed.
before: Connect your own S3, COS, R2, Amazon S3, or MinIO storage under Settings → Data.
The current device has a valid Pro license and can access the backup bucket.
Restoring changes local user data. Create another rollback backup of the current library first.

sections.title: 1. Open backup snapshots
sections.body:
Open the S3 cloud-backup area under Settings → Data, confirm that the connection is healthy, then open backup history.

If the connection test fails, do not start a restore. Check the endpoint, region, bucket, prefix, path style, and access credentials.

sections.title: 2. Select the correct snapshot
sections.body:
Select a snapshot using its creation time and device details. Prefer the last backup you verified as usable rather than choosing by the latest timestamp alone.

Before restoring, confirm again that the snapshot belongs to the correct library and account collection.

callout.title: Restore is not a preview
callout.body: After confirmation, local user data switches to the snapshot state. Current changes that have not been backed up may be lost.

sections.title: 3. Start the restore
sections.body:
Select Restore and read the confirmation carefully. Keep TradeReplay and the network connection active. Do not run an import, download, or backtest during the restore.

TradeReplay restores user data. Large official system-data files do not all need to be stored in each snapshot; download them again when needed after recovery.

sections.title: 4. Verify each area after recovery
bullets: Confirm live accounts, practice sessions, and trade counts.
Open systems, indicators, journals, and settings and check their latest modification times.
Open several trades with charts. Download official market data again if it is missing.
After every check passes, create a new cloud backup as the post-recovery baseline.

callout.title: Protect storage credentials
callout.body: Access keys and secrets are used only to connect to your storage. Do not capture them in screenshots, paste them into support requests, or send them to anyone. Use a dedicated least-privilege key and rotate it regularly.

success: Accounts, trades, strategies, journals, and settings match the target snapshot.
Missing official market data can be downloaded again and used for review.
A new post-recovery backup appears in history.

faq.q: Does restoring delete the cloud snapshot?
faq.a: No. Restore reads the selected snapshot; it does not clear the remote backup.

faq.q: Why must some market data be downloaded again?
faq.a: Cloud backup prioritizes irreplaceable user data. Official system data that can be obtained again may be downloaded after recovery to keep snapshots smaller.

faq.q: Can I restore a snapshot from another computer onto a new computer?
faq.a: Yes, provided the new computer can access the same storage and runs a compatible TradeReplay version. Confirm the target library location and license status before restoring.

articles.title: Activate Pro, check validity, and deactivate this device
articles.summary: Enter the purchase email and activation code, then manage the two-device allowance.
articles.outcome: The current computer will show Pro status, and you will know how to free an old device slot when switching computers.
before: Have the email used for purchase and the activation code you received.
Confirm that the computer can reach license.tradereplay.dev.
One activation code can be used on up to two devices at the same time.

sections.title: 1. Enter the email and activation code
sections.body:
Open Settings → License, enter the purchase email and activation code, then select Activate.

When copying, avoid leading or trailing spaces. The email must match the one used for purchase.

sections.title: 2. Check the license status
sections.body:
After successful activation, the page displays Pro, a perpetual license, or an expiry date. The main window also shows the Pro badge.

When a time-limited license expires, existing data is not deleted. New actions follow Free-plan limits.

sections.title: 3. Deactivate before changing devices
sections.body:
While the old computer is still available, open the License page and deactivate the current device. Then enter the same email and activation code on the new computer.

Deactivation frees a license slot; it does not delete the library on the old computer.

success: The License page shows Pro and the correct validity period.
The main window no longer asks for activation.
Deactivation releases the current device slot.

faq.q: What should I do when all device slots are in use?
faq.a: Deactivate a device you no longer use. If the old device is unavailable, contact official support so the purchase can be verified and the device slot handled.

faq.q: Does activation upload my trade data?
faq.a: No. Activation verifies the license and device allowance; it does not require uploading trade records.

articles.title: Market-data download fails or makes no progress
articles.summary: Check the network, license, range, disk, and data source in a safe order.
articles.outcome: You will troubleshoot failed, stalled, or unusable market-data downloads without damaging existing data.
before: Keep the current task and complete error message. Do not click Download repeatedly.
Confirm that the drive containing the library is still connected.
Do not delete library files manually.

sections.title: 1. Record the status and range
sections.body: Record the instrument, data type, date range, progress position, and complete error. Distinguish a task that never started, an interrupted download, a write failure, and data that cannot be read after completion.

sections.title: 2. Check network access
sections.body: Confirm that ordinary websites load, the system clock is correct, and no proxy, firewall, or security software blocks TradeReplay. If only one source fails, try again later and check whether the service is temporarily unavailable.

sections.title: 3. Check the range and license
sections.body: Confirm that the selected range is available for the instrument and included in the current license. Test a short range first, then expand it after success.

sections.title: 4. Check the disk and library
sections.body: Confirm there is enough disk space, the folder is writable, an external drive is connected, and the library is not in a synced folder. Do not move the library or let cleanup software remove temporary files during a download.

sections.title: 5. Retry safely
sections.body: Cancel a task that has clearly failed, reopen Market Data, and retry a shorter range. If it still fails, retain the error text, app version, instrument, and dates when contacting support.

callout.title: Do not delete the database
callout.body: A market-data download problem rarely requires deleting tradereplay.db. Manual deletion can lose trades and notes.

success: You can identify whether the failure occurs in the network, permission, range, or local write stage.
A short-range test succeeds, or you have saved reproducible error details.
Existing trades and the library remain intact.

faq.q: Can I click Download repeatedly when progress has not moved for a long time?
faq.a: No. Check whether processing is still active. Cancel a failed task, reopen the page, and retry once.

faq.q: Why can’t a new session find the data after the download finishes?
faq.a: Check whether the session uses System, Custom, or Tick data and whether the instrument and local date range are correct.

faq.q: What if changing networks does not fix it?
faq.a: Continue with the range, license, disk-space, and library-write checks. Keep the complete error when contacting support.

articles.title: Chart time differs from statement time by several hours
articles.summary: Distinguish broker time, the display time zone, daylight saving time, and underlying UTC data.
articles.outcome: You will distinguish statement time, chart display time, and underlying UTC, then verify the offset with a known fill.
before: Have an original fill with a clearly known time.
Record the time zone used by the broker server or report.
Do not hide an offset by manually editing fill times.

sections.title: 1. Distinguish the three time layers
sections.body: An original statement may use broker-server time. TradeReplay can store internal data in UTC, while charts display it in a selected time zone. The same instant can therefore show a different hour in each layer.

sections.title: 2. Identify a fixed or seasonal offset
sections.body: If the difference is the same throughout the year, the cause is usually the selected time zone. If it changes by one hour in only part of the year, daylight saving time is the likely cause.

sections.title: 3. Adjust the display or import interpretation
sections.body: Choose the correct time-zone basis in data, import, or chart settings, then check again. Do not add or subtract hours in several places, because that applies the offset twice.

sections.title: 4. Verify with a known event
sections.body: Select a trade with a known entry time and check whether its entry marker appears on the correct bar. Then spot-check one trade on each side of a daylight-saving transition.

callout.title: Fix the time zone even when the price matches
callout.body: An incorrect time affects sessions, calendars, holding duration, and statistical grouping.

success: You can explain the source of statement time and display time.
A known trade marker appears near the correct bar.
Checks before and after a daylight-saving transition both pass.

faq.q: Why is the difference always eight hours?
faq.a: A common cause is directly comparing UTC with China Standard Time. Confirm the report time zone and apply the conversion in only one place.

faq.q: Why is the offset different in winter and summer?
faq.a: The broker server or exchange may observe daylight saving time. Use a regional time zone with daylight-saving rules rather than a fixed UTC offset.

faq.q: Does the time zone change the fill price?
faq.a: It does not rewrite the original fill price, but it changes which chart bar the trade aligns with and how results are grouped by date or session.

articles.title: Activation code is invalid, expired, or out of device slots
articles.summary: Check the email, whitespace, network, validity period, and old device slots.
articles.outcome: You will troubleshoot the email, activation code, network, validity period, and device allowance for each error type, then contact support safely if needed.
before: Have the purchase email and complete activation code.
The computer is online and its system date and time are correct.
Never show the complete activation code in a public screenshot.

sections.title: 1. Activate from Settings
sections.body: Go to Settings → License and enter the purchase email and activation code. Copying is recommended, but check for leading spaces, trailing spaces, line breaks, and easily confused characters after pasting.

sections.title: 2. Invalid code or email mismatch
sections.body: Confirm that the email matches the purchase, no code characters are missing, and you did not enter an order number as the activation code. If Invalid remains, keep the error text instead of trying repeatedly.

sections.title: 3. Expired or revoked
sections.body: Check the license validity period and order status. After renewal or another purchase, use the corresponding new license details. A revoked code cannot be bypassed locally.

sections.title: 4. All device slots are in use
sections.body: One license supports up to two devices. Deactivate or release an old device first, then activate the new computer. Contact support if the old device is unavailable.

sections.title: 5. Contact support safely
sections.body: Provide the purchase email, app version, operating system, and complete error message. Share only a masked fragment of the activation code when necessary. Never send a password or verification code.

callout.title: Activation must reach the license service
callout.body: A proxy, firewall, incorrect system clock, or temporary network failure can prevent a valid license from being verified.

success: The License page shows the correct status and validity period.
You can identify whether the error is caused by input, validity, network, or the device allowance.
Any information shared externally has been masked.

faq.q: Why are all device slots used after moving to a new computer?
faq.a: The old device still occupies a slot. Deactivate it first. If that is impossible, contact support to verify the purchase and release the old record.

faq.q: Does reinstalling the operating system count as a new device?
faq.a: Device identification can change. If that triggers the limit, release the old record through device management.

faq.q: Can I activate for the first time while offline?
faq.a: No. First activation and status verification require a connection to the license service.

articles.title: Library cannot be opened, moved, or restored
articles.summary: Handle incomplete folders, newer library versions, synced drives, and integrity-check failures.
articles.outcome: You will address an incorrect library path, failed migration, newer library version, or integrity failure without overwriting the original data.
before: Quit TradeReplay and retain a complete copy of the affected library.
Check whether tradereplay.db exists in the library root.
Do not repeatedly move or overwrite the only copy.

sections.title: 1. Select the library root
sections.body: When opening an existing library, select the root folder containing tradereplay.db. Do not select the database file itself or a market-data or backup subfolder.

sections.title: 2. Check that the folder is complete
sections.body: A library should remain together as a whole. Copying only the database, omitting supporting folders, disconnecting an external drive, or leaving cloud placeholders can all prevent opening or migration.

sections.title: 3. Respond to version and integrity messages
sections.body: Library version is newer means the current app cannot safely read a library created by a later version. Update TradeReplay instead of forcing it open. If an integrity check fails, stop writing, retain the original, and restore from a verified backup first.

sections.title: 4. Migrate correctly
sections.body: Use the in-app library migration feature and select a new empty folder. TradeReplay copies and verifies the database, market data, and backups before switching. Do not quit, put the computer to sleep, or disconnect the drive during migration.

sections.title: 5. Restore from backup
sections.body: Restore into a new empty folder first; do not overwrite the affected original. Open the restored copy and spot-check accounts, trades, notes, and market data. Replace the everyday library only after every check passes.

callout.title: A synced drive is not a library backup strategy
callout.body: Synchronizing an active database can create conflicts or incomplete files. For remote protection, use a backup flow supported by TradeReplay.

success: A complete copy of the affected original library still exists.
The new location is empty and migration verification passes.
Accounts, trades, notes, and market data have been spot-checked after recovery.

faq.q: Can I drag tradereplay.db onto a new computer?
faq.a: Copying only one file is not recommended. A library also contains market data, backups, and related content. Move the complete library or use the in-app process.

faq.q: Why can I see files in a synced drive but not open them?
faq.a: They may be cloud placeholders, or the database and supporting files may be at different versions. Download everything and copy it into a new local folder before verifying.

faq.q: Can I keep importing after an integrity failure?
faq.a: No. Do not write more data to the affected library. Keep a copy, restore from a reliable backup, or contact support for assessment.
